```{r phase2_facet_definitions}
# measures the same construct through a different channel -- closed-ended items,
# external to the text -- which is what makes the correlation evidence of VALIDITY
# rather than of internal consistency.
FACET_SCALE_MAP <- c(
  desert          = "deserved",          # Retribution_1..4 (just-deserts purpose items)
  proportionality = "proportionality",   # the single proportionality item
  revenge         = "revenge",           # revenge_1..4
  suffering       = "suffering"          # suffer_1, suffer_2
)
# Facets with no admissible survey anchor can never clear clause B of the gate and
# are therefore reported as exploratory-only, never as support for a claim.
# That is censure and moral_balance (the instrument has no closed-ended censure or
# moral-balance scale) plus the three consequentialist facets (the goal subscales
# measure endorsement of a goal, not the language a person uses about it, so they
# are not the matching scale prereg 6.7 has in mind). This is a property of the
# instrument, decided before the data were seen; these five stay descriptive
# however their numbers come out.
NO_ANCHOR_FACETS <- setdiff(FACETS_ALL, names(FACET_SCALE_MAP))

# === THE TWO GATE THRESHOLDS (prereg 6.7, quoted verbatim in Phase 4) ===
# "A facet supports a claim only if the models agree at an intraclass correlation
#  of at least .60 AND the facet correlates at least .30 with its matching survey
#  scale."
# .60 is the conventional floor for treating a set of raters as interchangeable
# enough to average -- below it the ensemble mean is mostly rater noise, and the
# facet is not one measurement but several disagreeing ones.
# .30 is a moderate correlation: high enough that the facet and its scale are
# demonstrably about the same thing, low enough to be attainable across a change
# of measurement channel (free text vs 1-7 items) where nobody should expect the
# agreement of two parallel questionnaire forms.
# BOTH are required. AND, not OR: reliability without validity is an ensemble
# agreeing on the wrong construct, and validity without reliability is a
# correlation computed from an average nobody could reproduce.
ICC_MIN <- 0.60   # prereg 6.7 clause A: inter-model ICC
R_MIN   <- 0.30   # prereg 6.7 clause B: facet vs matching survey scale

# Printed up front, before any data exist, so the standard is on the record ahead
# of the numbers it will be applied to.
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    facet = FACETS_ALL,
    family = ifelse(FACETS_ALL %in% PRINCIPLED_FACETS, "principled retributive",
              ifelse(FACETS_ALL %in% VENGEFUL_FACETS, "vengeful", "consequentialist")),
    survey_anchor = ifelse(FACETS_ALL %in% names(FACET_SCALE_MAP),
                           FACET_SCALE_MAP[FACETS_ALL], "none - exploratory only"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "The nine facets and their preregistered survey anchors")
```

# PHASE 3: LOADING THE LANGUAGE STREAMS

Four streams feed the analysis: the **LLM ensemble** (primary scorer), the **word list**
(the non-model corroboration the prereg requires for E4), the **embedding similarities**
(convergence only, never a gate), and the **human gold codes**. The readers below are
deliberately tolerant about column naming, because the notebooks are still being built:
each looks for the expected key columns and reports what it found.

```{r phase3_load_ensemble}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3a: THE LLM ENSEMBLE FACET SCORES (the primary scorer)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads ensemble_facet_scores.csv, identifies the score
# column, and reshapes the long file (one row per response x item x facet) into
# the wide form the analysis uses (one row per response x item, one column per
# facet).
# PREREG: 6.7 -- "Coding is done by an ensemble of language models in place of
#         human raters... The facet score for a response is the average across
#         models." These scores carry every primary E3-E7 test.
# WRITES: ens_long (as read), ens_wide (the reshaped frame joined in Phase 3f).
#         May clear ENS_READY / GATE_READY / E_READY if the file is unusable.
#
# GUARD: ENS_READY. Before the ensemble notebook has run, this chunk prints the
# awaiting-Colab banner and both frames stay NULL, which is what makes every
# ens_* column absent from the join and every E-test fall through to its own
# banner.
# =========================================================================

ens_long <- NULL; ens_wide <- NULL

if (ENS_READY) {
  # guess_max = 100000 comfortably exceeds the expected row count (up to three
  # items x nine facets x 948 participants), so column types are inferred from
  # the whole file rather than a leading sample.
  ens_long <- readr::read_csv(NLP_PATHS[["ensemble"]], show_col_types = FALSE,
                              guess_max = 100000)
  cat(sprintf("ensemble_facet_scores.csv: %d rows x %d cols\n",
              nrow(ens_long), ncol(ens_long)))

  # The notebooks are the upstream authority on column naming, so the reader
  # accepts any of four plausible names for the across-model average and reports
  # which one it used. intersect() preserves the order of the candidate list, so
  # the most specific name wins if more than one is present.
  score_col <- intersect(c("ensemble_mean", "facet_score", "score", "mean"),
                         names(ens_long))[1]
  if (is.na(score_col)) {
    # Present but unusable. Clearing all three flags routes the rest of the
    # document into exactly the same awaiting-Colab state as a missing file,
    # rather than letting a nameless column produce NA facets that would silently
    # fail the gate and be read as a substantive result.
    cat("!! No recognised score column (ensemble_mean / facet_score / score / mean).\n")
    ens_long <- NULL; ENS_READY <- FALSE; GATE_READY <- FALSE; E_READY <- FALSE
  } else {
    cat(sprintf("  score column: %s\n", score_col))
    ens_wide <- ens_long %>%
      # .score is a positional alias for whichever column name was found, so the
      # pivot below does not have to be written four ways.
      dplyr::select(response_id, item_type, facet, .score = dplyr::all_of(score_col)) %>%
      # Drop any facet the notebook emits that is not in the preregistered scheme.
      # The nine facets of prereg 5.15 are the analysis; an extra experimental
      # category from the notebook must not silently become a tenth column.
      dplyr::filter(facet %in% FACETS_ALL) %>%
      # Long -> wide on facet. values_fn averages if a response x item x facet
      # ever appears more than once (e.g. a re-run appended rather than replaced);
      # without it pivot_wider would return list-columns and every downstream
      # numeric operation would fail in a hard-to-read way.
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = facet, values_from = .score,
                         values_fn = function(z) mean(z, na.rm = TRUE))
    # Print which facets actually arrived: a facet the notebook did not score is
    # simply absent here, and the E-tests below skip it rather than error.
    cat(sprintf("  wide ensemble frame: %d response x item rows, facets present: %s\n",
                nrow(ens_wide),
                paste(intersect(FACETS_ALL, names(ens_wide)), collapse = ", ")))
  }
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The LLM ensemble facet scores", NLP_FILES[["ensemble"]])
}
```

```{r phase3_load_agreement}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3b: THE CROSS-MODEL AGREEMENT TABLE (gate clause A)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads ensemble_agreement.csv and locates the ICC column
# that clause A of the 6.7 gate is evaluated on. Prints the whole table.
# PREREG: 6.7 -- "We report agreement across the models for each facet, an
#         intraclass correlation for the 0-to-1 scores and Krippendorff's alpha
#         for the categorical judgment, which plays the part that inter-rater
#         reliability plays with human coders."
# WRITES: agree_tbl, icc_col. May clear AGREE_READY / GATE_READY / E_READY.
#
# The models are the raters. This table is their reliability, and prereg 6.7 is
# explicit that it is reliability and NOT validity: models trained on similar data
# can share a bias, and the line between principled desert and revenge is exactly
# what this study is examining, so a high ICC on its own would only mean the
# models are consistently reading the corpus the same way -- possibly consistently
# wrong. That is why clause B exists.
#
# GUARD: AGREE_READY. Without this file the gate cannot be evaluated at all, and
# no facet can become claim-eligible.
# =========================================================================

agree_tbl <- NULL

if (AGREE_READY) {
  agree_tbl <- readr::read_csv(NLP_PATHS[["agreement"]], show_col_types = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("ensemble_agreement.csv: %d rows x %d cols\n",
              nrow(agree_tbl), ncol(agree_tbl)))
  # Candidate names in preference order. ICC(2,k) variants come first because the
  # relevant reliability is that of the AVERAGE across the k models -- which is
  # what the facet score actually is -- rather than of a single randomly chosen
  # model; a bare "icc"/"ICC" is accepted as a fallback and reported by name so
  # the printed table shows which coefficient the gate ran on.
  icc_col <- intersect(c("icc2k", "icc_2k", "ICC2k", "ICC_2k", "icc", "ICC",
                         "icc2_1", "icc21"), names(agree_tbl))[1]
  if (is.na(icc_col)) {
    # No ICC means clause A is unevaluable, and a facet cannot pass a two-clause
    # gate on one clause. Clearing the flags is the correct response -- treating a
    # missing ICC as a pass would let the whole validation step evaporate.
    cat("!! No recognised ICC column; clause A of the gate cannot be evaluated.\n")
    AGREE_READY <- FALSE; GATE_READY <- FALSE; E_READY <- FALSE
  } else {
    cat(sprintf("  ICC column used for gate clause A: %s\n", icc_col))
    # The full table is printed rather than just the column used, so a reader can
    # see the Krippendorff alpha for the holistic judgment and any per-model
    # diagnostics alongside the number the gate consumes.
    print(as.data.frame(agree_tbl), row.names = FALSE)
  }
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The cross-model agreement table (gate clause A, ICC >= .60)",
                 NLP_FILES[["agreement"]])
}
```

```{r phase3_load_dictionary}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3c: THE NON-MODEL WORD LIST (dictionary stream)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads facet_dictionary_scores.csv, confirms the
# per-100-word rate columns are present, and prints how often each facet fires in
# each item.
# PREREG: 6.7 -- the word list is the first of the two non-model safeguards, "whose
#         retributive entries are wider than the Dark Side list and whose known
#         false matches are removed, so the adverb 'just' no longer counts toward
#         desert and no word counts toward two opposing facets".
# WRITES: dict_long -- consumed by the E4 corroboration (Phase 6), the E3 preview
#         (Phase 5), E5's sparsity check (Phase 7) and E6's second stream.
#
# WHY THIS STREAM EXISTS AND WHAT IT MAY NOT DO. Because the word list uses no
# language model, its agreement with the ensemble is a more independent check than
# the models' agreement with one another -- which is why prereg 6.7 REQUIRES it
# for E4 specifically. But it is a corroboration stream, not a test: it never
# gates a facet, never carries a headline, and its results are never registered
# in the FDR family.
#
# GUARD: DICT_READY. This stream can arrive independently of the ensemble
# (different notebook), so several chunks below can print real word-list numbers
# while the ensemble half still shows the awaiting-Colab banner.
# =========================================================================

dict_long <- NULL

if (DICT_READY) {
  dict_long <- readr::read_csv(NLP_PATHS[["dictionary"]], show_col_types = FALSE,
                               guess_max = 100000)
  cat(sprintf("facet_dictionary_scores.csv: %d rows x %d cols\n",
              nrow(dict_long), ncol(dict_long)))
  # Expect the three item types (backward, forward, ranking) and up to 948 ids.
  cat(sprintf("  item types: %s\n", paste(unique(dict_long$item_type), collapse = ", ")))
  cat(sprintf("  responses:  %d unique response_id\n", length(unique(dict_long$response_id))))

  # Rates per 100 words are the analysis unit; raw counts are word-count confounded.
  # A raw hit count rises with length for any facet, so correlating two raw counts
  # measures verbosity. Normalising per 100 words removes the mechanical part; the
  # part_cor() word-count covariate then removes what normalisation misses (facet
  # density itself can vary with length).
  per100 <- paste0(FACETS_ALL, "_per100")
  have100 <- intersect(per100, names(dict_long))
  cat(sprintf("  per-100-word columns present: %d of %d\n", length(have100), length(per100)))

  # Prevalence, not mean rate: the share of non-blank responses with AT LEAST ONE
  # hit. For a sparse dictionary that is the more honest summary -- a mean rate
  # near zero cannot distinguish "everyone uses a little" from "almost nobody uses
  # any", and only the second makes a null uninterpretable.
  prev <- dict_long %>%
    # Blank responses would otherwise enter the denominator as guaranteed
    # non-hits and deflate every prevalence figure by the skip rate.
    dplyr::filter(n_words > 0) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(item_type) %>%
    # mean(.x > 0) over a logical is the proportion of responses with >= 1 hit;
    # x100 makes it a percentage. Facets absent from the file are skipped via
    # intersect() rather than producing an error.
    dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(intersect(FACETS_ALL, names(dict_long))),
                                   ~ round(100 * mean(.x > 0, na.rm = TRUE), 1)),
                     .groups = "drop")
  cat("\nWord-list prevalence (% of non-blank responses with >= 1 hit), by item:\n")
  print(as.data.frame(prev), row.names = FALSE)
  cat("\nNOTE: the word list is the NON-MODEL corroboration stream. It never gates a\n")
  cat("facet and never carries a headline; the prereg uses it only to check that E4's\n")
  cat("co-occurrence is not an artifact of one method assigning several facets at once.\n")
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The word-list (dictionary) facet scores", NLP_FILES[["dictionary"]])
}
```

```{r phase3_load_embedding}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3d: EMBEDDING SIMILARITIES (convergence evidence only)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads embedding_facet_similarity.csv, finds the one
# similarity column per embedding model, and reports the two things prereg 6.7
# says to report about them -- the shift in absolute level between models, and the
# stability of the ordering.
# PREREG: 6.7 -- the second non-model safeguard: "similarity to short reference
#         passages for each facet, computed with more than one embedding model".
#         And: "the absolute level of the similarity scores shifts across
#         embedding models while the ordering of responses stays stable, and we
#         report that for the facet scores as well".
# WRITES: emb_long -- averaged across models and joined as emb_* in Phase 3f.
#
# THIS STREAM NEVER GATES ANYTHING. It is reported as convergence and nothing
# more: no clause of the 6.7 gate reads it, no E-test is registered from it, and
# it never stands alone as a result.
#
# GUARD: EMB_READY.
# =========================================================================

emb_long <- NULL

if (EMB_READY) {
  emb_long <- readr::read_csv(NLP_PATHS[["embedding"]], show_col_types = FALSE,
                              guess_max = 100000)
  cat(sprintf("embedding_facet_similarity.csv: %d rows x %d cols\n",
              nrow(emb_long), ncol(emb_long)))
  # One "*_sim" column per embedding model. Discovering them by suffix rather than
  # by a fixed list keeps the reader working when a model is added or swapped.
  sim_cols <- grep("_sim$", names(emb_long), value = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("  similarity columns: %s\n", paste(sim_cols, collapse = ", ")))
  if (length(sim_cols) >= 2) {
    cat("\nAbsolute level shifts across embedding models (expected), with the\n")
    cat("rank-order stability that actually matters:\n")
    # The means differ across models because cosine similarity has no absolute
    # meaning -- each embedding space has its own typical similarity between any
    # two pieces of English. A level difference here is expected and is not a
    # disagreement.
    print(round(sapply(emb_long[sim_cols], mean, na.rm = TRUE), 3))
    # SPEARMAN, not Pearson: what has to hold is that the models ORDER responses
    # the same way, which is a monotone question. Pearson would additionally
    # penalise a model for using a compressed range, which is exactly the
    # difference the line above establishes is meaningless. Pairwise-complete so
    # one model's missing score does not drop the row from every other pair.
    print(round(stats::cor(emb_long[sim_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs",
                           method = "spearman"), 3))
  }
  cat("\nNOTE: embeddings are convergence evidence only. Per prereg 6.7 they never\n")
  cat("gate a facet and never stand alone as a result.\n")
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The embedding facet similarities (convergence only)",
                 NLP_FILES[["embedding"]])
}
```

```{r phase3_load_gold}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3e: HUMAN GOLD CODES AND THE FROZEN SEED/TEST SPLIT
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads the adjudicated human codes and the split
# assignment, and reports the shape of each.
# PREREG: 6.7 supplies the principle that agreement among models is reliability
#         rather than validity, but it prescribes no human coding -- it has the
#         ensemble score "in place of human raters". The human gold set is therefore
#         an ADDITION to the registered plan, carried on the OSF addendum and listed
#         in the deviation table in NLP/MEASUREMENT_DESIGN.md. The preregistered
#         validation gate itself is untouched: inter-model ICC and the facet-to-scale
#         correlation are what license a facet.
# WRITES: gold_codes, gold_split. Both are loaded and described here; the
#         human-versus-ensemble comparison itself belongs to the Colab side.
#
# WHY THE SPLIT IS FROZEN BEFORE SCORING. SEED responses feed the things that are
# TUNED -- the embedding reference passages, the lexicon expansion, the rubric
# anchors. TEST responses feed every validation number. Freezing the assignment
# before any scoring happens is what keeps the validation out of sample: a
# reference passage chosen because it worked on a response would otherwise be
# validated on that same response.
#
# GUARDS: GOLD_READY and SPLIT_READY, tested separately because the two files can
# arrive independently.
# =========================================================================

gold_codes <- NULL; gold_split <- NULL

if (GOLD_READY) {
  gold_codes <- readr::read_csv(NLP_PATHS[["gold"]], show_col_types = FALSE,
                                guess_max = 100000)
  cat(sprintf("gold_codes.csv: %d rows x %d cols\n", nrow(gold_codes), ncol(gold_codes)))
  # The column list is printed rather than assumed: the coding scheme is settled
  # upstream, and this is where a reader confirms which facets were adjudicated.
  cat(sprintf("  columns: %s\n", paste(names(gold_codes), collapse = ", ")))
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The adjudicated human gold codes", NLP_FILES[["gold"]])
}

if (SPLIT_READY) {
  gold_split <- readr::read_csv(NLP_PATHS[["goldsplit"]], show_col_types = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("\ngold_split_assignment.csv: %d rows\n", nrow(gold_split)))
  sp_col <- intersect(c("gold_split", "split", "assignment"), names(gold_split))[1]
  # useNA = "ifany" surfaces unassigned rows: a response in the gold set with no
  # SEED/TEST label is neither tuning material nor validation material, and the
  # count is the only place that would show.
  if (!is.na(sp_col)) print(table(gold_split[[sp_col]], useNA = "ifany"))
  cat("\nThe SEED/TEST split is frozen before scoring: SEED feeds embedding references,\n")
  cat("lexicon expansion and rubric anchors; TEST feeds every validation number.\n")
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The frozen SEED/TEST split assignment", NLP_FILES[["goldsplit"]])
}
```

```{r phase3_join}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3f: THE JOINED ANALYSIS FRAME
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds `facets_joined`, the single frame every E-test
# reads -- one row per response_id x item_type, carrying whichever facet streams
# arrived, the word-count covariate, and the participant-level survey validators.
# PREREG: 6.7 (the facets are validated against, and analysed alongside, the
#         closed-ended scales).
# WRITES: survey_join, facets_joined, BACKWARD_ITEMS.
#
# NOTE THE GRAIN. facets_joined is at RESPONSE x ITEM grain, while the survey is
# at PARTICIPANT grain, so each participant's survey values are repeated across
# their (up to three) text rows. That is what makes a within-item analysis a
# one-line filter, but it also means any participant-level statistic computed
# straight off this frame would be weighted by how many items that person
# answered. Where a participant-level number is wanted -- gate clause B is the
# case in point -- the code aggregates to response_id first.
#
# The frame is built unconditionally, starting from texts_long. Before any Colab
# output exists it still has its response_id / item_type / n_words / nonblank
# spine plus the sv_* survey columns, and simply no ens_*, dict_* or emb_*
# columns; the counts printed at the foot of the chunk read 0 / 0 / 0.
# =========================================================================

# The joined analysis frame: one row per response_id x item_type, carrying the
# facet streams, the word-count covariate, and the participant-level survey
# validators. Built whenever at least one facet stream exists.
survey_join <- survey %>%
  dplyr::select(response_id = ResponseId, Vignette, retributivist, retribution,
                retribution_rel, punitiveness, punitiveness_full, Sentence1_z,
                Sentence1, Sentence2, sentence_ratio, deserved, proportionality,
                proportionality_jd, revenge, suffering, just_deserts,
                # Shark_3 (how painful the death should be) is optional: it is
                # only needed by the secondary E7 check, and any_of() lets the
                # join succeed on a scored file that predates it.
                dplyr::any_of("Shark_3"))
# Prefix the survey validators so they can never collide with a facet of the same
# name (the survey has `revenge` and `suffering`; so does the facet scheme).
# THIS PREFIX IS LOAD-BEARING. Without it, joining the survey `revenge` scale to
# the `revenge` facet would leave dplyr to disambiguate with .x/.y suffixes, and
# gate clause B -- which correlates the facet against the scale -- could silently
# end up correlating one of them with itself. From here on, sv_ always means the
# closed-ended survey scale and ens_/dict_/emb_ always mean scored text.
names(survey_join)[names(survey_join) != "response_id"] <-
  paste0("sv_", names(survey_join)[names(survey_join) != "response_id"])

# Start from the corpus spine, so the frame has one row per open-ended response
# whether or not any facet stream exists.
facets_joined <- texts_long %>%
  dplyr::select(response_id, item_type, orientation, vignette, n_words, nonblank)

# --- Stream 1: the ensemble (ens_*) -- the primary scorer ------------------
# left_join keeps every corpus row, so a response the notebook did not score
# becomes NA rather than disappearing. That matters: a silent inner join would
# shrink the denominator of every later percentage without saying so.
if (!is.null(ens_wide)) {
  facets_joined <- facets_joined %>%
    dplyr::left_join(ens_wide %>%
                       dplyr::rename_with(~ paste0("ens_", .x),
                                          dplyr::any_of(FACETS_ALL)),
                     by = c("response_id", "item_type"))
}
# --- Stream 2: the word list (dict_*) -- the non-model corroboration -------
# The per-100-word rate columns are selected and the "_per100" suffix stripped,
# so dict_desert lines up name-for-name with ens_desert and the two streams can
# be run through the same loops.
if (!is.null(dict_long)) {
  dcols <- intersect(paste0(FACETS_ALL, "_per100"), names(dict_long))
  facets_joined <- facets_joined %>%
    dplyr::left_join(dict_long %>%
                       dplyr::select(response_id, item_type, dplyr::all_of(dcols)) %>%
                       dplyr::rename_with(~ paste0("dict_", sub("_per100$", "", .x)),
                                          dplyr::all_of(dcols)),
                     by = c("response_id", "item_type"))
}
# --- Stream 3: the embeddings (emb_*) -- convergence only ------------------
if (!is.null(emb_long)) {
  sim_cols <- grep("_sim$", names(emb_long), value = TRUE)
  # The key-column test is a guard against an embedding file in a different shape
  # (say, one row per model). Without all three keys the pivot below is not
  # meaningful, and skipping is better than joining something misaligned.
  if (length(sim_cols) && all(c("response_id", "item_type", "facet") %in% names(emb_long))) {
    emb_wide <- emb_long %>%
      # Average the similarity across embedding models into one score per facet.
      # Averaging is defensible precisely because of the Spearman check printed in
      # Phase 3d: the models differ in level but agree in ordering, so the mean is
      # a sensible summary of a consistent ranking rather than a blend of two
      # different opinions.
      dplyr::mutate(.sim = rowMeans(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(sim_cols)), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      dplyr::select(response_id, item_type, facet, .sim) %>%
      dplyr::filter(facet %in% FACETS_ALL) %>%
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = facet, values_from = .sim,
                         values_fn = function(z) mean(z, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      dplyr::rename_with(~ paste0("emb_", .x), dplyr::any_of(FACETS_ALL))
    facets_joined <- facets_joined %>%
      dplyr::left_join(emb_wide, by = c("response_id", "item_type"))
  }
}

# Finally attach the participant-level survey validators. Joined by response_id
# ALONE (not response_id x item_type), which is what repeats each participant's
# scale scores across their text rows.
facets_joined <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::left_join(survey_join, by = "response_id")

# The four counts below are the quickest read on what state the document is in:
# all three facet counts at 0 with a non-zero survey count means the survey side
# is complete and the language side is awaiting Colab.
cat(sprintf("Joined analysis frame: %d rows x %d columns\n",
            nrow(facets_joined), ncol(facets_joined)))
cat(sprintf("  ensemble columns:   %d\n", sum(grepl("^ens_",  names(facets_joined)))))
cat(sprintf("  word-list columns:  %d\n", sum(grepl("^dict_", names(facets_joined)))))
cat(sprintf("  embedding columns:  %d\n", sum(grepl("^emb_",  names(facets_joined)))))
cat(sprintf("  survey validators:  %d\n", sum(grepl("^sv_",   names(facets_joined)))))

# Backward-looking rows (Q1 and Q333) are the E3/E4/E5 corpus; they are kept
# separate, never pooled into one passage (prereg 5.15). Every E-test uses this
# constant to select ROWS one item at a time and reports each result per item,
# because averaging the two would mix two different questions -- why this sentence,
# and why this ranking -- into a single passage. The one place it deliberately
# aggregates across both is gate clause B, where the facet score has to be
# participant-level to correlate against a participant-level survey scale; that
# aggregation is a property of the gate, not of the hypothesis tests.
BACKWARD_ITEMS <- c("backward", "ranking")
```

```{r phase3_fig_prevalence, fig.height=5}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 3g: FIGURE -- WORD-LIST FACET PREVALENCE BY ITEM
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: plots the share of non-blank responses containing at
# least one word-list hit, per facet per item.
# PREREG: 6.7 (the non-model word list). Descriptive; not a test of anything and
#         not registered in the FDR family.
# WRITES: output/figures/wordlist_facet_prevalence.png
#
# WHY IT IS WORTH A FIGURE. It is the evidence for how the word list may be read.
# A facet that fires in a small minority of responses cannot support a stable
# correlation, so a near-zero word-list r for that facet is uninformative rather
# than negative. Phase 7 turns this into an explicit 10% rule for E5.
#
# fig.height = 5 overrides the document default of 7: nine facets x three items
# is a wide, short plot, and the taller default leaves a band of whitespace.
# GUARD: DICT_READY.
# =========================================================================

if (DICT_READY) {
  prev_long <- dict_long %>%
    dplyr::filter(n_words > 0) %>%
    # Wide -> long so facet can become an aesthetic. intersect() means facets the
    # notebook did not emit are simply not plotted.
    tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(intersect(FACETS_ALL, names(dict_long))),
                        names_to = "facet", values_to = "hits") %>%
    dplyr::group_by(item_type, facet) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(pct = 100 * mean(hits > 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    # Explicit factor levels rather than alphabetical order: facets are ordered
    # principled -> vengeful -> consequentialist (the FACETS_ALL order), and the
    # items backward -> ranking -> forward, which puts the two backward-looking
    # items side by side so the eye can compare them before reaching the
    # forward-looking one.
    dplyr::mutate(facet = factor(facet, levels = FACETS_ALL),
                  item_type = factor(item_type,
                                     levels = c("backward", "ranking", "forward")))

  p_prev <- ggplot2::ggplot(prev_long,
                            ggplot2::aes(x = facet, y = pct, fill = item_type)) +
    ggplot2::geom_col(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .8), width = .75) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = "Word-list facet prevalence by open-ended item",
      subtitle = "Non-model dictionary stream; sparse facets are why it corroborates rather than tests",
      x = NULL, y = "% of non-blank responses with >= 1 hit", fill = "Item") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    # Facet names are long; the 30-degree rotation keeps them legible without the
    # vertical labels a 90-degree rotation would give.
    ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
  print(p_prev)
  # Saved as well as printed: the knitted HTML embeds it, and the PNG in
  # output/figures/ is what goes into a manuscript or onto OSF.
  ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "wordlist_facet_prevalence.png"),
                  p_prev, width = 10, height = 5, dpi = 200)
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The word-list prevalence figure", NLP_FILES[["dictionary"]])
}
```

# PHASE 4: THE PRE-REGISTERED §6.7 VALIDATION GATE

> "A facet supports a claim only if the models agree at an intraclass correlation of at
> least .60 **and** the facet correlates at least .30 with its matching survey scale."
> — prereg §6.7

Two clauses, both required:

  - **Clause A (reliability)** — inter-model ICC ≥ `r sprintf("%.2f", 0.60)`, read from
    `ensemble_agreement.csv`. Agreement among models is *reliability, not validity*:
    models trained on similar data can share a bias, and the desert/revenge boundary is
    exactly what this study is examining.
  - **Clause B (external validity)** — the facet correlates ≥ `r sprintf("%.2f", 0.30)`
    with its matching survey scale, **word count partialled**, at the routed item. The
    survey scales are external to the text, which is what makes this clause do work that
    clause A cannot.

The two clauses are joined by **and**, not by *or*, and neither substitutes for the other.
Clause A alone would certify an ensemble that agrees with itself about the wrong
construct — three models trained on overlapping corpora can share a bias, and the very
distinction this study exists to test, principled desert versus revenge, is one where a
shared prior is likely. Clause B alone would certify a correlation computed from an
average that no one could reproduce: if the models disagree, the facet score is a
different number each time it is scored, and its correlation with anything is an accident
of that particular run.

The four anchored pairings are fixed by prereg §6.7 and are not chosen after seeing the
data: desert → `deserved` (the just-deserts purpose items, Retribution 1–4),
proportionality → the single `proportionality` item, revenge → the `revenge` scale,
suffering → the `suffer` items. Each survey scale is external to the text, which is what
makes clause B a validity check rather than another internal-consistency check.

Facets with **no admissible survey anchor** — censure and moral balance, plus the three
consequentialist facets — cannot clear clause B by construction. They are reported as
**exploratory descriptives only** and never used to support a claim. This is settled by
what the instrument measures, not by how their numbers come out.

The gate governs what a result may be *used for*; it does not decide which tests are run
or which enter the FDR correction. A facet that fails still appears in the tables below,
still enters the Benjamini–Hochberg family, and is still reported honestly — it simply
supports no claim. Those are two different questions, and keeping them apart is what stops
a small *p*-value from being mistaken for a valid measurement.

```{r phase4_gate_spec}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 4a: THE GATE SPECIFICATION, STATED BEFORE IT IS EVALUATED
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: prints, per facet, exactly what it would have to do to
# pass -- the ICC threshold and the named survey scale with its r threshold.
# PREREG: 6.7, both clauses.
# WRITES: gate_spec, and the printed specification table.
#
# This runs unguarded and therefore prints in full even before the ensemble
# exists. That is the point of putting it in its own chunk: the standard is on the
# record ahead of the numbers, and the five no-anchor facets are visibly marked as
# unable to clear clause B before anyone has seen how they scored.
# =========================================================================

gate_spec <- data.frame(
  facet = FACETS_ALL,
  clause_A = sprintf("inter-model ICC >= %.2f", ICC_MIN),
  clause_B = ifelse(FACETS_ALL %in% names(FACET_SCALE_MAP),
                    sprintf("r >= %.2f with survey '%s' (word count partialled)",
                            R_MIN, FACET_SCALE_MAP[FACETS_ALL]),
                    "NO ADMISSIBLE SURVEY ANCHOR - exploratory only"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(gate_spec, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "The two gate clauses, per facet (prereg 6.7)")
```

```{r phase4_gate_eval}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 4b: EVALUATING THE 6.7 GATE
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: computes both clauses for all nine facets and assigns
# each a status of PASS, FAIL, or EXPLORATORY (no anchor).
# PREREG: 6.7 -- "A facet supports a claim only if the models agree at an
#         intraclass correlation of at least .60 and the facet correlates at
#         least .30 with its matching survey scale."
# WRITES: gate_table; output/tables/gate_table.csv.
#
# CLAUSE A is read from the agreement table: inter-model ICC >= ICC_MIN (.60).
# CLAUSE B is computed here: the partial correlation between the facet and its
#   matching survey scale, word count partialled, at the backward-looking items,
#   >= R_MIN (.30).
#
# BOTH REQUIRED, AND THE THRESHOLDS ARE ONE-SIDED IN THE OBVIOUS DIRECTION: a
# facet passes clause B on r >= .30, not on |r| >= .30. A facet that correlated
# -.45 with the scale it is supposed to be measuring has not been validated, it
# has been shown to run backwards, and treating that as a pass would let a
# sign-flipped scorer through the one check designed to catch it.
#
# ELSE BRANCH: when the ensemble or agreement table is missing, an all-NA gate
# table of the same shape is built and written anyway, so the CSV always exists
# and downstream tooling has a stable target. Every anchored facet reads
# "AWAITING COLAB OUTPUTS" and every unanchored one reads "EXPLORATORY (no survey
# anchor)" -- the second is a permanent fact about the instrument, not a
# consequence of the pipeline not having run.
#
# GUARD: GATE_READY (= ENS_READY && AGREE_READY).
# =========================================================================

gate_table <- NULL

if (GATE_READY) {

  # Re-resolved here rather than carried from Phase 3b so this chunk can be run on
  # its own in an interactive session without leaving icc_col undefined.
  icc_col <- intersect(c("icc2k", "icc_2k", "ICC2k", "ICC_2k", "icc", "ICC",
                         "icc2_1", "icc21"), names(agree_tbl))[1]

  # ICC per facet; if the agreement table is split by item_type, take the value at
  # the routed (backward-looking) item, else the single value.
  #' @param f  facet name
  #' @return   the facet's inter-model ICC, or NA if the table has no such row
  #'
  #' Routing to the backward-looking items matters: reliability is a property of
  #' the models scoring THIS corpus, and the corpus clause B is computed on is the
  #' backward-looking one. Averaging in the forward item's ICC would let good
  #' agreement about deterrence language prop up poor agreement about desert.
  #' Where the notebook reports one ICC per facet with no item breakdown, the
  #' single value is used unchanged.
  get_icc <- function(f) {
    a <- agree_tbl[agree_tbl$facet == f, , drop = FALSE]
    if (!nrow(a)) return(NA_real_)
    if ("item_type" %in% names(a) && any(a$item_type %in% BACKWARD_ITEMS)) {
      a <- a[a$item_type %in% BACKWARD_ITEMS, , drop = FALSE]
    }
    # as.numeric guards against the column arriving as character (a stray "NA" or
    # a thousands separator); suppressWarnings absorbs the expected coercion note.
    mean(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(a[[icc_col]])), na.rm = TRUE)
  }

  # Clause B: facet at the backward-looking items vs its survey scale, word count
  # partialled. Participant-level aggregation over the backward items (Q1, Q333).
  gate_rows <- lapply(FACETS_ALL, function(f) {
    ens_col <- paste0("ens_", f)
    icc <- get_icc(f)
    # A facet with no entry in FACET_SCALE_MAP has no admissible anchor; anchor
    # stays NA and clause B is never attempted for it.
    anchor <- if (f %in% names(FACET_SCALE_MAP)) FACET_SCALE_MAP[[f]] else NA_character_
    # Pre-seeded with the same shape part_cor() returns, so the data.frame at the
    # foot of the function has its columns whether or not clause B ran.
    r <- data.frame(r = NA_real_, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, p = NA_real_, n = 0L)

    if (!is.na(anchor) && ens_col %in% names(facets_joined)) {
      # AGGREGATE TO THE PARTICIPANT FIRST. The survey scale is a participant-level
      # score, so the correlation has to be participant-level too. Correlating at
      # response x item grain would enter each participant twice (Q1 and Q333) with
      # their scale value repeated, which inflates n, understates the standard
      # error, and turns a within-person consistency into apparent between-person
      # agreement.
      agg <- facets_joined %>%
        dplyr::filter(item_type %in% BACKWARD_ITEMS, nonblank) %>%
        dplyr::group_by(response_id) %>%
        # facet_score: mean across whichever backward items the person answered.
        # n_words: SUMMED, not averaged -- the covariate should represent the total
        #   volume of text the facet score was computed from, which is what drives
        #   the opportunity to trip a facet.
        # scale_score: first() because the survey value is constant within
        #   response_id; mean() would give the same number, first() says why.
        dplyr::summarise(facet_score = mean(.data[[ens_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
                         n_words = sum(n_words, na.rm = TRUE),
                         scale_score = dplyr::first(.data[[paste0("sv_", anchor)]]),
                         .groups = "drop")
      r <- part_cor(agg$facet_score, agg$scale_score, agg$n_words)
    }

    # The !is.na() wrappers make a missing value a FAIL rather than an NA that
    # would propagate into the status test and land in the else branch anyway --
    # explicit is better here, because "we could not evaluate this" and "this
    # failed" both mean the facet supports no claim.
    clause_A <- !is.na(icc) && icc >= ICC_MIN
    clause_B <- !is.na(r$r) && r$r >= R_MIN
    # Three statuses, and the order of the tests matters: the no-anchor check comes
    # FIRST, so an unanchored facet is never labelled a failure. It did not fail
    # the gate; the instrument gives it nothing to be validated against.
    status <- if (is.na(anchor)) {
      "EXPLORATORY (no survey anchor)"
    } else if (clause_A && clause_B) {
      "PASS - may support a claim"
    } else {
      "FAIL - descriptive only"
    }
    data.frame(facet = f, survey_anchor = ifelse(is.na(anchor), "-", anchor),
               icc = icc, clause_A_icc = clause_A,
               r_survey = r$r, r_lo = r$lo, r_hi = r$hi, r_p = r$p, n = r$n,
               clause_B_r = clause_B, status = status, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
  gate_table <- do.call(rbind, gate_rows)

  # The table reports the INPUTS to both clauses (icc, r with its CI, p, n) next
  # to the booleans and the verdict, so a reader can see how near a miss a FAIL
  # was rather than only that it failed.
  print(knitr::kable(gate_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
                     caption = "Section 6.7 validation gate"))
  readr::write_csv(gate_table, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "gate_table.csv"))
  cat(sprintf("\nWrote %s\n", file.path(OUT_TABLES, "gate_table.csv")))

} else {
  # Same columns, same facet order, all NA. Written to the same path so the CSV
  # exists in both states and nothing downstream has to branch on its presence.
  gate_table <- data.frame(
    facet = FACETS_ALL,
    survey_anchor = ifelse(FACETS_ALL %in% names(FACET_SCALE_MAP),
                           FACET_SCALE_MAP[FACETS_ALL], "-"),
    icc = NA_real_, clause_A_icc = NA, r_survey = NA_real_, r_lo = NA_real_,
    r_hi = NA_real_, r_p = NA_real_, n = NA_integer_, clause_B_r = NA,
    status = ifelse(FACETS_ALL %in% names(FACET_SCALE_MAP),
                    "AWAITING COLAB OUTPUTS", "EXPLORATORY (no survey anchor)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print(knitr::kable(gate_table, row.names = FALSE,
                     caption = "Section 6.7 validation gate (not yet evaluable)"))
  readr::write_csv(gate_table, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "gate_table.csv"))
  cat("\n")
  awaiting_colab("The 6.7 validation gate",
                 c(NLP_FILES[["ensemble"]], NLP_FILES[["agreement"]]))
}
```

```{r phase4_gate_facets}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 4c: THE GATE-PASSING FACET SET
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reduces the gate table to GATE_PASS, the character vector
# of facets a claim may rest on, and says plainly what it means when it is empty.
# PREREG: 6.7.
# WRITES: GATE_PASS -- read by every register_test() call in Phases 5-9 (as
#         claim_eligible) and by E7's predictor selection in Phase 9.
#
# GATE_PASS is the single point of contact between the validation step and the
# hypothesis tests. Nothing downstream re-derives it, so a facet's claim status is
# decided once, here, from the printed table.
# =========================================================================

# The facets any E3-E7 CLAIM may rest on. Everything else is descriptive.
# The any(!is.na(clause_A_icc)) test distinguishes "the gate ran and nothing
# passed" from "the gate never ran": in the awaiting-Colab table every
# clause_A_icc is NA, and the status column carries the placeholder text rather
# than a verdict, so matching on status alone would be reading a label that was
# never earned. Both cases yield character(0), but only for the right reason.
GATE_PASS <- if (!is.null(gate_table) && any(!is.na(gate_table$clause_A_icc))) {
  gate_table$facet[gate_table$status == "PASS - may support a claim"]
} else character(0)

cat("Gate-passing facets (claims may rest on these):\n")
if (length(GATE_PASS)) {
  cat(sprintf("  %s\n", paste(GATE_PASS, collapse = ", ")))
} else {
  cat("  none yet - the gate has not been evaluated.\n")
  cat("  Until it is, every facet result below is DESCRIPTIVE and supports no claim.\n")
}
```

```{r phase4_gate_figure, fig.height=5}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 4d: FIGURE -- THE GATE AS A PLANE
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: plots every facet in the ICC x survey-r plane, with the
# pass region shaded and both thresholds drawn as dashed lines.
# PREREG: 6.7.
# WRITES: output/figures/gate_icc_by_survey_r.png
#
# The figure makes the conjunction visual: only the upper-right rectangle passes,
# and a facet sitting just outside one line is visibly a near miss on ONE clause
# rather than a general failure. It also makes the two failure modes legible at a
# glance -- high ICC with low r is the models agreeing about something the survey
# does not recognise; low ICC with high r is a correlation resting on an
# unreliable average.
#
# GUARD: GATE_READY plus at least one non-NA r_survey -- an all-NA plane would
# render as an empty panel, which reads as a broken figure rather than as a
# pending one, so the awaiting-Colab banner is printed instead.
# =========================================================================

if (GATE_READY && any(!is.na(gate_table$r_survey))) {
  # Keep any facet with at least one coordinate. A no-anchor facet has an ICC but
  # no r, so it drops out of the plot at the geom stage; it stays in the printed
  # table above, where its status is stated in words.
  gt <- gate_table[!is.na(gate_table$icc) | !is.na(gate_table$r_survey), ]
  p_gate <- ggplot2::ggplot(gt, ggplot2::aes(x = icc, y = r_survey, label = facet)) +
    # The shaded rectangle IS the gate: x >= .60 AND y >= .30, unbounded above.
    # Drawn first so the points sit on top of it.
    ggplot2::geom_rect(xmin = ICC_MIN, xmax = Inf, ymin = R_MIN, ymax = Inf,
                       fill = "grey90", colour = NA) +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = ICC_MIN, linetype = "dashed") +
    ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = R_MIN, linetype = "dashed") +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3) +
    # Labels sit just above their points so a cluster near a threshold stays
    # readable.
    ggplot2::geom_text(vjust = -0.9, size = 3.5) +
    ggplot2::labs(title = "Section 6.7 validation gate",
                  subtitle = sprintf("Shaded region: ICC >= %.2f AND r >= %.2f with the matching survey scale",
                                     ICC_MIN, R_MIN),
                  x = "Inter-model ICC", y = "r with matching survey scale (word count partialled)") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  print(p_gate)
  ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "gate_icc_by_survey_r.png"),
                  p_gate, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 200)
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The gate figure (ICC x survey-r plane)",
                 c(NLP_FILES[["ensemble"]], NLP_FILES[["agreement"]]))
}
```

# PHASE 5: E3 — RETRIBUTIVISTS VERSUS OTHERS ON THE BACKWARD-LOOKING TEXTS

**E3 (exploratory).** In the backward-looking explanations — the sentence justification
(**Q1**, `item_type == "backward"`) and the goal-ranking explanation (**Q333**,
`item_type == "ranking"`) — retributivists use more desert, proportionality, and censure
language than non-retributivists.

Two forms, both run: (a) the **categorical** contrast, retributivists
(`Prioritization_1 == 1`) versus everyone else, Welch *t* with Cohen's *d*; and (b) the
**continuous** form, a regression of the facet on the **relative retribution subscale**
(the primary continuous measure of prereg §5.3), with **word count** as a covariate.
Q1 and Q333 are analysed **separately, never pooled** — the two backward items act as a
within-study replication of each other.

Both retributivist measures are used because prereg §5.3 expects any single one to be
imperfect: participants may report the goals they take to be socially expected, people
often punish on desert while describing utilitarian aims, and introspective access to a
punitive motive is limited. The categorical and continuous forms fail differently, so
agreement between them is informative and disagreement is worth seeing rather than
averaging away.

```{r phase5_e3}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 5: E3 -- RETRIBUTIVIST LANGUAGE IN THE BACKWARD-LOOKING TEXTS
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: for each backward-looking item and each of five facets,
# runs (a) a Welch contrast of retributivists against everyone else on the
# word-count-adjusted facet score and (b) a regression of the facet on the
# relative retribution subscale with word count covaried. Registers both in the
# exploratory family.
# PREREG: 2.4 (E3), 6.7 ("For E3 we compare facet scores between retributivists
#         and others, and regress them on the retribution subscale, using the
#         backward-looking texts"), 5.3 (both retributivist measures).
# WRITES: e3_results; output/tables/e3_backward_facets.csv; 2 x items x facets
#         rows appended to FAMILY.
#
# EXPLORATORY. E3 is one of the five predictions in the single exploratory family;
# nothing here is confirmatory, and the p-values in the printed table are raw --
# the BH-adjusted values that carry the inference appear in Phase 10.
#
# GUARD: E_READY. Before the ensemble exists this prints the awaiting-Colab
# banner and registers nothing, which is why the Phase 10 family is empty.
# =========================================================================

e3_results <- NULL

if (E_READY) {

  # E3 names desert, proportionality and censure. The two vengeful facets are run
  # alongside them not because E3 predicts anything about them, but because the
  # interesting comparison is whether retributivists' language is MORE principled
  # in particular or simply more punitive across the board; without the vengeful
  # facets in the same table that question cannot be read off the results.
  e3_facets <- intersect(c(E4_PRINCIPLED, VENGEFUL_FACETS), FACETS_ALL)
  rows <- list()

  # Outer loop: one item at a time (prereg 5.15 -- Q1 and Q333 never pooled).
  for (it in BACKWARD_ITEMS) {
    dd <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::filter(item_type == it, nonblank)
    for (f in e3_facets) {
      ens_col <- paste0("ens_", f)
      # A facet the ensemble did not score is skipped rather than fabricated.
      if (!ens_col %in% names(dd)) next

      # (a) categorical: retributivist vs rest, word count residualised out first
      # The covariate cannot enter a t-test directly, so it is removed first by
      # regressing the facet on n_words and testing the residuals. That is the
      # same adjustment the regression in (b) makes internally, applied here so
      # the group contrast is covariate-adjusted too -- prereg 6.7 makes word
      # count a covariate throughout, not only in the regression form.
      y_raw <- dd[[ens_col]]
      ok <- stats::complete.cases(y_raw, dd$n_words)
      # y_adj is pre-filled with NA and written only at the complete rows, so the
      # residual vector stays aligned with dd's rows and lines up with
      # sv_retributivist below. Building it from resid() alone would silently
      # shift the group labels against the scores.
      y_adj <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(dd))
      if (sum(ok) > 5) y_adj[ok] <- stats::resid(stats::lm(y_raw[ok] ~ dd$n_words[ok]))
      # Welch rather than Student: the retributivist group is a minority of the
      # sample, so the two ns are unequal, and equal variances are not something
      # to assume when one group may talk about desert both more and more
      # variably. See welch_d() in Phase 0c.
      wd <- welch_d(y_adj, dd$sv_retributivist)

      # (b) continuous: regression on the relative retribution subscale + word count
      # retribution_rel is prereg 5.3's primary CONTINUOUS measure -- retribution
      # minus the mean of the other three goals -- so this form does not depend on
      # where the categorical split falls, and it uses the whole sample rather
      # than contrasting two groups. Word count enters as a second predictor,
      # which is the same adjustment (a) makes by residualising.
      m <- tryCatch(stats::lm(y_raw ~ dd$sv_retribution_rel + dd$n_words),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
      b <- se <- pval <- NA_real_
      # Row 2 of the coefficient matrix is sv_retribution_rel (row 1 is the
      # intercept, row 3 is n_words). The nrow() check catches a model that
      # collapsed to an intercept because the predictor had no variance.
      if (!is.null(m) && nrow(stats::coef(summary(m))) >= 2) {
        cf <- stats::coef(summary(m))[2, ]
        b <- cf[["Estimate"]]; se <- cf[["Std. Error"]]; pval <- cf[["Pr(>|t|)"]]
      }

      # One row per item x facet carrying BOTH forms side by side, plus the gate
      # verdict, so a reader never sees an E3 effect without seeing whether the
      # facet behind it was validated.
      rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        item = it, facet = f, gate = ifelse(f %in% GATE_PASS, "PASS", "not gated"),
        M_other = wd$M0, M_retributivist = wd$M1, t = wd$t, p_group = wd$p, d = wd$d,
        b_retrib_rel = b, se = se, p_reg = pval, n = wd$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

      # Both forms are registered separately: they are two tests, they can
      # disagree, and BH must see the true number of tests in the family.
      # The d interval uses the large-sample approximation SE(d) ~ sqrt(4/n),
      # which is the standard 2/sqrt(n) form; max(n, 2) keeps it finite if a
      # degenerate cell ever returned n = 0.
      register_test("E3", sprintf("%s | %s | retributivist vs rest (word count adj.)", it, f),
                    "Cohen's d", wd$d,
                    wd$d - 1.96 * sqrt(4 / max(wd$n, 2)), wd$d + 1.96 * sqrt(4 / max(wd$n, 2)),
                    wd$p, wd$n, claim_eligible = f %in% GATE_PASS)
      # The regression CI is the conventional b +/- 1.96 SE.
      register_test("E3", sprintf("%s | %s | ~ relative retribution + word count", it, f),
                    "b", b, b - 1.96 * se, b + 1.96 * se, pval, wd$n,
                    claim_eligible = f %in% GATE_PASS)
    }
  }
  e3_results <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  if (!is.null(e3_results)) {
    print(knitr::kable(e3_results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
                       caption = "E3: backward-looking facet language, Q1 and Q333 separately"))
    readr::write_csv(e3_results, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "e3_backward_facets.csv"))
  }

} else {
  awaiting_colab("E3 (retributivists vs others on the backward-looking texts)",
                 c(NLP_FILES[["ensemble"]], NLP_FILES[["agreement"]]))
}
```

```{r phase5_e3_wordlist_preview}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 5b: E3 WORD-LIST PREVIEW (descriptive)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs the E3 group contrast on the non-model word-list
# scores instead of the ensemble, for the three principled facets.
# PREREG: 6.7 (the word list as a non-model stream). This is NOT the E3 test:
#         prereg 6.7 tests E3 on the facet scores, and reserves the word list for
#         corroboration.
# WRITES: prev_tbl; output/tables/e3_wordlist_preview.csv. Registers NOTHING.
#
# WHY IT IS HERE AND WHY IT IS NOT IN THE FAMILY. The word list is scored by a
# different notebook and can arrive before the ensemble, so this is often the
# first E3-shaped number the document can produce. It is worth seeing -- if the
# word list shows nothing at all, the ensemble result deserves more scepticism --
# but it is descriptive, so registering it would add rows to the BH denominator
# for a test nobody will claim from, costing power on the tests that matter.
#
# THE `&& !E_READY` IS DELIBERATE. Once the ensemble arrives, the real E3 test
# above supersedes this preview and it stops printing, so the two never sit in
# the output together where a reader might take the preview for the result.
# =========================================================================

# NON-MODEL PREVIEW. The word list is not the E3 test and is not registered in the
# FDR family; it is shown because it can be computed now and it is the same stream
# the prereg relies on for the E4 corroboration.
if (DICT_READY && !E_READY) {
  cat("DICTIONARY PREVIEW (non-model word list) - descriptive only, not the E3 test,\n")
  cat("not in the FDR family. Rates per 100 words, non-blank responses.\n\n")

  prev_rows <- list()
  for (it in BACKWARD_ITEMS) {
    dd <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::filter(item_type == it, nonblank)
    for (f in intersect(E4_PRINCIPLED, FACETS_ALL)) {
      dcol <- paste0("dict_", f)
      if (!dcol %in% names(dd)) next
      # No word-count residualisation here, unlike the ensemble version above: the
      # dictionary columns are already rates per 100 words, so the mechanical part
      # of the length effect is normalised out at source. That also means these
      # numbers are not on the same scale as the ensemble d's and should not be
      # compared to them digit for digit -- the preview answers whether the
      # direction is there, not whether the magnitude matches.
      wd <- welch_d(dd[[dcol]], dd$sv_retributivist)
      prev_rows[[length(prev_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
        item = it, facet = f, M_other = wd$M0, M_retributivist = wd$M1,
        t = wd$t, p = wd$p, d = wd$d, n = wd$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    }
  }
  if (length(prev_rows)) {
    prev_tbl <- do.call(rbind, prev_rows)
    print(knitr::kable(prev_tbl, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
                       caption = "E3 word-list preview (descriptive; NOT the E3 test)"))
    readr::write_csv(prev_tbl, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "e3_wordlist_preview.csv"))
  }
} else if (!DICT_READY) {
  awaiting_colab("The E3 word-list preview", NLP_FILES[["dictionary"]])
}
```

# PHASE 6: E4 — PRINCIPLED AND VENGEFUL LANGUAGE TOGETHER

**E4 (exploratory).** Within participants, principled-retributive language (**desert,
proportionality, censure**) appears **together with** vengeful language (**revenge,
infliction of suffering**) rather than in place of it. A positive correlation between the
two across responses would show that ordinary just deserts is bound up with revenge.

The prereg does not accept the ensemble correlation on its own:

> "Because both sides come from the same automated scoring, one method's tendency to
> assign several facets at once could create this correlation on its own, so **we require
> the same co-occurrence to show up in the non-model word-list measure**, and **we compare
> it with the relationship between the desert and revenge scales in the survey**, before
> reading it as evidence…" — prereg §6.7

So three numbers are reported side by side: the **ensemble** correlation (the test), the
**word-list** correlation (the required non-model corroboration), and the **survey**
`r(deserved, revenge)` benchmark. Word count is partialled throughout.

```{r phase6_e4_ensemble}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 6a: E4 -- PRINCIPLED x VENGEFUL CO-OCCURRENCE (the ensemble arm)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: per backward-looking item, averages the three principled
# facets and the two vengeful ones into two composites and correlates them with
# word count partialled; then prints the facet-by-facet breakdown behind that
# composite correlation.
# PREREG: 2.4 (E4), 6.7 ("For E4 we estimate the correlation across responses
#         between the principled facets (desert, proportionality, censure) and
#         the vengeful facets (revenge, suffering)").
# WRITES: e4_rows (the ensemble entries); one FAMILY row per item.
#
# WHAT THE NUMBER WOULD MEAN. A POSITIVE correlation is the predicted result and
# the substantive claim: people who reach for desert language also reach for
# revenge language, so ordinary just deserts is bound up with getting even rather
# than standing apart from it. A null would say the two vocabularies are
# independent -- principled retributive talk is its own thing. A negative
# correlation would say they substitute for each other.
#
# WHY THE ENSEMBLE NUMBER CANNOT BE READ ALONE. Both sides come from the same
# scorer, and one method's tendency to assign several facets to a rich response
# would produce a positive correlation by itself. That is why prereg 6.7 REQUIRES
# the word-list corroboration in the next chunk before this is read as evidence.
#
# GUARD: E_READY.
# =========================================================================

e4_rows <- list()

if (E_READY) {
  for (it in BACKWARD_ITEMS) {
    dd <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::filter(item_type == it, nonblank)
    pcols <- intersect(paste0("ens_", E4_PRINCIPLED), names(dd))
    vcols <- intersect(paste0("ens_", E4_VENGEFUL),   names(dd))
    # Both sides need at least one facet present or there is no correlation to
    # compute; skip the item rather than emit a spurious NA row.
    if (!length(pcols) || !length(vcols)) next

    # The two composites are unweighted row means of the facets on each side --
    # the sides the prereg names, three principled and two vengeful. na.rm keeps a
    # response contributing when the ensemble scored some facets but not others.
    dd$principled <- rowMeans(dd[, pcols, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
    dd$vengeful   <- rowMeans(dd[, vcols, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
    # Word count partialled: without it, a long response scores higher on both
    # composites simply by containing more material, and the correlation would
    # largely be a correlation between length and length.
    pc <- part_cor(dd$principled, dd$vengeful, dd$n_words)

    e4_rows[[length(e4_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      stream = "ensemble (LLM)", item = it, r = pc$r, lo = pc$lo, hi = pc$hi,
      p = pc$p, n = pc$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    # claim_eligible requires at least one gate-passing facet on EACH side: a
    # correlation between a validated principled composite and an unvalidated
    # vengeful one is a correlation with something whose meaning is unestablished,
    # so it cannot carry the claim either.
    register_test("E4", sprintf("%s | principled x vengeful (ensemble, word count partialled)", it),
                  "partial r", pc$r, pc$lo, pc$hi, pc$p, pc$n,
                  claim_eligible = any(E4_PRINCIPLED %in% GATE_PASS) &&
                                   any(E4_VENGEFUL %in% GATE_PASS))

    # Facet-by-facet detail: which principled facet travels with which vengeful one.
    # The composite correlation can hide its own composition -- a strong
    # desert x revenge link with nothing else would produce much the same number
    # as three uniformly moderate links, and those are different findings. Printed
    # only, not registered: these six cells are a decomposition of the test above,
    # not six additional tests, and registering them would multiply E4's weight in
    # the BH family sixfold for one prediction.
    detail <- expand.grid(p = E4_PRINCIPLED, v = E4_VENGEFUL, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    det_rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(detail)), function(i) {
      pc_i <- part_cor(dd[[paste0("ens_", detail$p[i])]],
                       dd[[paste0("ens_", detail$v[i])]], dd$n_words)
      data.frame(item = it, principled = detail$p[i], vengeful = detail$v[i],
                 r = pc_i$r, lo = pc_i$lo, hi = pc_i$hi, p = pc_i$p, n = pc_i$n)
    })
    print(knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, det_rows), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
                       caption = sprintf("E4 detail (%s): each principled facet x each vengeful facet", it)))
  }
} else {
  awaiting_colab("E4 (ensemble principled x vengeful co-occurrence)",
                 c(NLP_FILES[["ensemble"]], NLP_FILES[["agreement"]]))
}
```

```{r phase6_e4_wordlist}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 6b: E4 -- THE REQUIRED NON-MODEL CORROBORATION
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: repeats the principled x vengeful correlation on the
# word-list scores, and reports the co-firing base rates that say whether that
# correlation could have been detected at all.
# PREREG: 6.7 -- "we require the same co-occurrence to show up in the non-model
#         word-list measure ... before reading it as evidence that ordinary just
#         deserts is bound up with revenge."
# WRITES: word-list entries appended to e4_rows. Registers NOTHING -- this is the
#         corroboration condition on E4, not a second test of it.
#
# THIS IS A PRECONDITION, NOT A ROBUSTNESS CHECK. The prereg makes the word-list
# result a requirement for reading the ensemble result as evidence. If the
# ensemble shows co-occurrence and the word list does not, the honest reading is
# that the co-occurrence may be an artifact of one scorer assigning several facets
# to the same rich response -- unless the base rates below show the word list was
# too sparse to have found it either way.
#
# GUARD: DICT_READY, tested independently of E_READY, so the corroboration can be
# computed and printed even while the ensemble arm is still awaiting Colab.
# =========================================================================

# THE REQUIRED NON-MODEL CORROBORATION. This runs on the word list, which uses no
# language model, so its agreement with the ensemble is a more independent check
# than the models' agreement with one another (prereg 6.7).
if (DICT_READY) {
  for (it in BACKWARD_ITEMS) {
    dd <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::filter(item_type == it, nonblank)
    pcols <- intersect(paste0("dict_", E4_PRINCIPLED), names(dd))
    vcols <- intersect(paste0("dict_", E4_VENGEFUL),   names(dd))
    if (!length(pcols) || !length(vcols)) next

    # Built exactly as the ensemble composites were, on the same facet sets and
    # the same items, so the two rows of the summary table differ only in scorer.
    dd$principled_wl <- rowMeans(dd[, pcols, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
    dd$vengeful_wl   <- rowMeans(dd[, vcols, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
    # Word count is partialled here too even though these are already per-100-word
    # rates: normalising removes the mechanical length effect, but facet DENSITY
    # can still vary with length (a longer answer may be more elaborated as well
    # as longer), and that residual path is what the covariate closes.
    pc <- part_cor(dd$principled_wl, dd$vengeful_wl, dd$n_words)

    e4_rows[[length(e4_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      stream = "word list (non-model)", item = it, r = pc$r, lo = pc$lo, hi = pc$hi,
      p = pc$p, n = pc$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }

  # Base rates matter here: the word list is structurally sparse on revenge, so a
  # near-zero correlation can be absence of signal rather than absence of
  # co-occurrence. Report the co-firing base rate alongside the correlation.
  #
  # HOW TO READ THE THREE PERCENTAGES. pct_both is the share of responses where at
  # least one principled facet AND at least one vengeful facet fired. If that is
  # near zero, the word-list correlation carries almost no information: the
  # co-occurrence the prereg asks it to corroborate had essentially no opportunity
  # to appear, and a null there does not undercut the ensemble result. If pct_both
  # is substantial and the correlation is still null, the corroboration has
  # genuinely failed and E4 cannot be read as evidence.
  # Descriptive; not registered.
  cofire <- facets_joined %>%
    dplyr::filter(item_type %in% BACKWARD_ITEMS, nonblank) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(item_type) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      pct_any_principled = 100 * mean(rowSums(dplyr::across(
        dplyr::any_of(paste0("dict_", E4_PRINCIPLED))) > 0, na.rm = TRUE) > 0),
      pct_any_vengeful = 100 * mean(rowSums(dplyr::across(
        dplyr::any_of(paste0("dict_", E4_VENGEFUL))) > 0, na.rm = TRUE) > 0),
      pct_both = 100 * mean(
        rowSums(dplyr::across(dplyr::any_of(paste0("dict_", E4_PRINCIPLED))) > 0, na.rm = TRUE) > 0 &
        rowSums(dplyr::across(dplyr::any_of(paste0("dict_", E4_VENGEFUL))) > 0, na.rm = TRUE) > 0),
      .groups = "drop")
  print(knitr::kable(cofire, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
                     caption = "Word-list co-firing base rates (a near-zero r may be sparsity, not independence)"))
} else {
  awaiting_colab("The required non-model word-list corroboration for E4",
                 NLP_FILES[["dictionary"]])
}
```

```{r phase6_e4_summary}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 6c: E4 -- THE THREE STREAMS SIDE BY SIDE
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: appends the survey benchmark to the ensemble and
# word-list rows and prints all three in one table, then restates the condition
# prereg 6.7 places on reading the ensemble estimate as evidence.
# PREREG: 6.7 -- "we compare it with the relationship between the desert and
#         revenge scales in the survey ... before reading it as evidence".
# WRITES: e4_results; output/tables/e4_principled_vengeful.csv.
#
# This chunk is UNGUARDED, and that is deliberate: the survey benchmark is always
# available, so the table always prints with at least one row. In the
# awaiting-Colab state it contains the survey benchmark alone, which is exactly
# the information a reader needs -- the yardstick, visible before the thing being
# measured arrives.
#
# WHY ALL THREE BELONG IN ONE TABLE. The ensemble r is the estimate, the word-list
# r is the precondition on reading it, and the survey r is the scale it is read
# against. Reported separately, an ensemble r of .35 looks like a finding;
# reported next to a survey r(deserved, revenge) of similar size it looks like the
# text reproducing what the closed-ended items already say, and next to a survey r
# near zero it looks like something the questionnaire missed.
# =========================================================================

# Survey benchmark, always available. Computed back in Phase 1c from the
# closed-ended scales alone, so it does not depend on any Colab output.
e4_rows[[length(e4_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
  stream = "survey benchmark", item = "r(deserved, revenge)",
  r = bench_desert_revenge$r, lo = bench_desert_revenge$lo,
  hi = bench_desert_revenge$hi, p = bench_desert_revenge$p,
  n = bench_desert_revenge$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

e4_results <- do.call(rbind, e4_rows)
print(knitr::kable(e4_results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
                   caption = "E4: principled x vengeful co-occurrence across the three streams"))
readr::write_csv(e4_results, file.path(OUT_TABLES, "e4_principled_vengeful.csv"))

cat("\nReading rule (prereg 6.7): the ensemble correlation is read as evidence that\n")
cat("ordinary just deserts is bound up with revenge ONLY IF the same co-occurrence\n")
cat("appears in the non-model word-list stream, and it is interpreted against the\n")
cat("survey r(deserved, revenge) shown above rather than in isolation.\n")
if (!E_READY) {
  cat("\nThe ensemble row is still missing, so no E4 reading is available yet.\n")
}
```

# PHASE 7: E5 — DESERT VERSUS PROPORTIONALITY LANGUAGE (TEXT VERSION OF H6)

**E5 (exploratory).** Desert language and proportionality language do not hold together in
the open-ended responses. This is the **text version of H6**, which asks the same question
of the closed-ended items: does "just deserts" cohere as one construct, or are *deserved*
and *proportionate* two different things people say?

The text estimate is reported next to the survey H6 correlation
`r(deserved, proportionality_jd)`, computed above. One caution belongs with it, and it
is ours rather than the registration's: proportionality language is rare, so a near-zero
text correlation can be a **null-by-absence** (nobody wrote proportionality language)
rather than evidence of two independent constructs. Base rates are reported with the
correlation for exactly that reason, and the standing of the proportionality facet is set
out in the deviation table in `NLP/MEASUREMENT_DESIGN.md`.

```{r phase7_e5}
# =========================================================================
# PHASE 7: E5 -- DESERT VERSUS PROPORTIONALITY LANGUAGE (the text version of H6)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: correlates desert language with proportionality language
# per backward-looking item, computes the alpha of the two together, repeats both
# on the word list with a sparsity check, and prints all of it beside the survey
# H6 correlation.
# PREREG: 2.4 (E5), 6.7 ("For E5 we test whether desert and proportionality
#         language hold together, the text version of H6"), 6.4 (H6 itself).
# WRITES: e5_results; output/tables/e5_desert_proportionality.csv; one FAMILY row
#         per item.
#
# THE INCOHERENCE IS THE FINDING. H6 predicts that just deserts does NOT hold
# together -- that "punishment is deserved" and "punishment should be
# proportionate" are two different things people believe, not two indicators of
# one construct. E5 asks the same of the language. So a NEAR-ZERO CORRELATION AND
# A LOW ALPHA ARE THE PREDICTED OUTCOME, not a measurement failure and not a null
# result to be apologised for. A reader who sees alpha of .10 here should read it
# as the hypothesis being borne out.
#
# THE ASYMMETRY WITH THE 6.7 GATE. The same low alpha would be a problem if this
# were a scale being built; it is not. E5 is testing whether the two cohere, and
# the gate's clause B -- which does require each facet to correlate .30 with its
# OWN survey anchor -- is what establishes that desert and proportionality are
# each measured well enough for their non-correlation to mean something. Failing
# to cohere with each other and succeeding at tracking their own anchors are
# exactly compatible, and together they are the result.
#
# THE COMPETING EXPLANATION. Proportionality language is rare. A near-zero
# correlation between a common facet and one almost nobody uses is a null BY
# ABSENCE, not evidence of two independent constructs, so the base rates are
# printed with the estimate and Phase 11 sets a 10% floor for reading it either
# way.
#
# GUARD: E_READY for the ensemble arm; DICT_READY for the word-list arm; the
# survey row and the printed table are unguarded.
# =========================================================================

e5_rows <- list()

if (E_READY) {
  for (it in BACKWARD_ITEMS) {
    dd <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::filter(item_type == it, nonblank)
    # Both facets required: E5 is about the relationship between them, so one
    # alone gives nothing.
    if (!all(c("ens_desert", "ens_proportionality") %in% names(dd))) next
    # Two-sided, via part_cor()'s default. E5 predicts the ABSENCE of a
    # relationship rather than a direction, and prereg 6.8 reserves one-sided
    # tests for predictions that name one -- an absence names none.
    pc <- part_cor(dd$ens_desert, dd$ens_proportionality, dd$n_words)
    e5_rows[[length(e5_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      stream = "ensemble (LLM)", item = it, r = pc$r, lo = pc$lo, hi = pc$hi,
      p = pc$p, n = pc$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    # BOTH facets must have cleared the gate for this to be claim-eligible: a
    # non-correlation between two things only means they are distinct if each is
    # known to measure something.
    register_test("E5", sprintf("%s | desert x proportionality language (word count partialled)", it),
                  "partial r", pc$r, pc$lo, pc$hi, pc$p, pc$n,
                  claim_eligible = all(c("desert", "proportionality") %in% GATE_PASS))

    # Alpha of the two text facets, the direct text analogue of the H6 alpha.
    # H6 reports the correlation, the alpha of the two together, and a
    # confirmatory factor model (prereg 6.4); the first two carry over to text
    # directly, so both are reported here.
    # scale() puts the two facets on a common metric first, because raw alpha is
    # computed from covariances and would otherwise be dominated by whichever
    # facet the ensemble happened to score on a wider range.
    # check.keys = FALSE is essential: with two items, psych::alpha's auto-reversal
    # would flip proportionality the moment the correlation went negative and
    # report a healthy alpha for a scale it had just inverted -- converting the
    # exact result E5 is looking for into its opposite.
    a <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(psych::alpha(
      data.frame(d = as.numeric(scale(dd$ens_desert)),
                 p = as.numeric(scale(dd$ens_proportionality))),
      check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha),
      error = function(e) NA_real_)
    cat(sprintf("%s: alpha of {desert, proportionality} language = %s (low alpha => does NOT cohere)\n",
                it, ifelse(is.na(a), "NA", sprintf("%.3f", a))))
  }
} else {
  awaiting_colab("E5 (desert vs proportionality language, the text version of H6)",
                 c(NLP_FILES[["ensemble"]], NLP_FILES[["agreement"]]))
}

# The word-list arm: the same question asked of the non-model stream. Not
# registered -- corroboration, as everywhere else in this document. Note that the
# word list is the stream where the sparsity problem bites hardest, which is why
# the prevalence of proportionality is printed on the same line as the estimate.
if (DICT_READY) {
  for (it in BACKWARD_ITEMS) {
    dd <- facets_joined %>% dplyr::filter(item_type == it, nonblank)
    if (!all(c("dict_desert", "dict_proportionality") %in% names(dd))) next
    pc <- part_cor(dd$dict_desert, dd$dict_proportionality, dd$n_words)
    e5_rows[[length(e5_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      stream = "word list (non-model)", item = it, r = pc$r, lo = pc$lo, hi = pc$hi,
      p = pc$p, n = pc$n, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    # The 10% floor: below it, too few responses contain any proportionality
    # language for a correlation to be estimable, and the flag printed on this
    # line marks the estimate as a null-by-absence at the point of reading rather
```
